US.83.def: President Lyndon B. Johnson's 1960s domestic program to end poverty and racial injustice and expand education, health care, and civil rights.
LBJ's set of Great Society programs — including Head Start and Job Corps — created in 1964 to reduce poverty in the United States.
Federal health-insurance programs created in 1965: Medicare for Americans 65 and older, Medicaid for low-income families.
A 1965 Great Society program providing early childhood education, health, and nutrition services to low-income children.
Federal programs that cleared and rebuilt city neighborhoods; often displaced poor and minority residents despite new housing and highways.

US.83.es: Ley de Derecho al Voto de 1965
US.83.def: A Great Society law that banned literacy tests and other barriers used to deny African Americans the right to vote.

US.84.def: A 1960s youth movement that rejected mainstream values, embracing new music, dress, and views on peace, freedom, and social change.
The sharp differences in values, politics, and culture between 1960s youth and their parents' generation.
A counterculture group of the 1960s that promoted peace, love, communal living, and opposition to the Vietnam War.
A 1969 music festival in New York that drew 400,000 people and became a symbol of the counterculture and antiwar spirit.
Widespread 1960s-70s protests, especially on college campuses, against U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War.
A 1960s political movement of young activists who pushed for civil rights, free speech, and an end to the Vietnam War.

US.85.def: President Nixon's term for the many Americans who quietly supported his policies but did not join loud public protests.
Nixon's policy of easing Cold War tensions with the Soviet Union and China through diplomacy and treaties.
Nixon's historic 1972 trip that reopened U.S. relations with Communist China after more than 20 years of hostility.
The 1972 Strategic Arms Limitation Talks treaty that limited U.S. and Soviet nuclear missiles, a key result of détente.
A Nixon program returning federal tax money to state and local governments to spend on their own priorities.
A federal agency created under Nixon in 1970 to write and enforce laws protecting air, water, and land.

US.86.def: A political scandal beginning with a 1972 break-in at Democratic headquarters that exposed abuses of power and forced Nixon to resign in 1974.
A 1974 Supreme Court ruling that the president is not above the law and must release the Watergate tapes.
A president's claimed right to keep some communications secret — rejected by the Court in the Watergate tapes case.
President Gerald Ford's 1974 decision to pardon Nixon for any crimes, a choice that deepened public distrust of government.
The constitutional process for charging a president with serious wrongdoing; Nixon resigned before the House could impeach him.
In-depth reporting — like the Washington Post's Watergate coverage — that uncovers hidden wrongdoing by those in power.

US.87.def: A movement that grew in the 1960s-70s to protect nature and public health from pollution and industrial harm.
The federal agency created in 1970 to set and enforce standards for clean air, water, and land.
First held April 22, 1970, a nationwide event that raised public awareness and support for protecting the environment.
A New York neighborhood built on buried toxic waste; its 1978 health crisis spurred federal cleanup laws like Superfund.
A 1979 partial nuclear meltdown in Pennsylvania that heightened fears about nuclear power safety.
A landmark law (expanded 1970) authorizing the federal government to limit air pollution from industry and vehicles.

US.88.def: An unusual 1970s economy combining high inflation, high unemployment, and slow growth at the same time.
1970s fuel shortages and soaring gas prices, worsened by an OPEC oil embargo, that strained the U.S. economy.
A 1978 peace agreement between Egypt and Israel brokered by President Carter, a major diplomatic success.
Carter-era treaties (1977) agreeing to hand control of the Panama Canal over to Panama by the year 2000.

US.88.es: Crisis de los Rehenes en Irán
US.88.def: The 1979-81 seizure of 52 Americans at the U.S. embassy in Iran for 444 days, which damaged Carter's presidency.
Carter's foreign policy of pressuring other nations to respect their citizens' basic rights.

US.89.def: President Reagan's economic plan of tax cuts, reduced regulation, and lower domestic spending to spur growth (supply-side economics).
The theory behind Reaganomics that cutting taxes on businesses and the wealthy encourages investment and benefits the whole economy.
Reagan's proposed 1983 space-based missile-defense system, nicknamed 'Star Wars,' to intercept Soviet nuclear attacks.
A 1980s scandal in which officials secretly sold arms to Iran and used the money to fund rebels in Nicaragua.
Expanded 1980s federal efforts to stop drug use and trafficking through tougher laws and enforcement.
The public-health crisis of the 1980s from a deadly new disease; the government's slow response drew wide criticism.

US.90.def: A 1991 U.S.-led coalition war that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait after Iraq's 1990 invasion.
The 1991 military campaign that quickly liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.
The 1989 opening of the wall dividing East and West Berlin, a symbol of the Cold War's end.
The 1991 breakup of the USSR into independent nations, ending the Cold War.
The 1989 U.S. military action that removed Panamanian dictator Manuel Noriega from power.
A 1990 law signed by President Bush banning discrimination against people with disabilities.

US.91.def: The 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement removing most trade barriers among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
A 1996 Clinton-era law that limited welfare benefits and required recipients to find work.
A federal budget in which spending does not exceed revenue; achieved in the late 1990s under Clinton.
The 1998 House impeachment of President Clinton for perjury and obstruction; the Senate acquitted him in 1999.
A 1994 Republican campaign plan led by Newt Gingrich promising smaller government and balanced budgets.
The late-1990s surge in internet-based businesses and stock values, which later crashed in 2000-01.

US.92.def: Coordinated al-Qaeda terrorist attacks that destroyed the World Trade Center and struck the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people.
The U.S. global campaign after 9/11 to defeat terrorist groups and the nations that harbored them.
A 2001 law expanding government surveillance powers to prevent terrorism, criticized by some as a threat to civil liberties.
A federal department created in 2002 to coordinate protection of the U.S. against terrorism and disasters.
The U.S. war begun in 2001 to remove the Taliban and destroy al-Qaeda bases after the 9/11 attacks.
The 2003 U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, launched on claims of weapons of mass destruction.

US.93.def: The first woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court, appointed in 1981.
The first African American U.S. Secretary of State (2001) and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The first African American woman U.S. Secretary of State (2005), a key foreign-policy leader.
U.S. Senator, Secretary of State, and the first woman to win a major party's presidential nomination (2016).
The first woman elected Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives (2007).
An invisible barrier that has kept women and minorities from reaching the highest positions in business and government.

US.94.def: The rapid late-20th-century spread of the internet, transforming how people communicate, work, and access information.
A system of linked web pages, opened to the public in the 1990s, that made the internet easy to use.
An affordable home computer that became common in the 1980s-90s, changing work, school, and daily life.
Online platforms of the 2000s that let people share content and connect instantly around the world.
A mobile phone with internet and computer features, widespread after 2007, that put communication in every pocket.
The gap between those who have reliable access to computers and the internet and those who do not.

US.95.es: Ley de Cuidado de Salud Asequible
US.95.def: President Obama's 2010 health-care law ('Obamacare') expanding insurance coverage to millions of Americans.
The severe 2007-09 economic downturn — the worst since the Great Depression — marked by a housing and banking crisis.
A 2009 stimulus law that used federal spending and tax cuts to fight the Great Recession.
Barack Obama, elected in 2008, whose presidency was a historic milestone in U.S. history.
The 2011 U.S. special-forces raid that killed the al-Qaeda leader behind the 9/11 attacks.
Sharp division between Democrats and Republicans that blocked lawmaking during much of Obama's presidency.
